I used Postman for 18 months. Thought I was doing API testing. Then a senior interviewer asked me one question. I had no answer.

"How do you validate that your API hasn't broken its contract with 3 downstream consumers?"

I said: "I'd check the response in Postman."
He nodded. Interview ended shortly after.

That failure taught me what API testing actually means at a senior level.

What juniors answer:
- Send request → check status code → check response body
What seniors answer:
- Contract validation across consumers
- Schema drift detection
- State injection to remove UI dependency
- Mocking downstream failures to test resilience
- Performance degradation thresholds, not just pass or fail

The difference isn't tools. It's the questions you know to ask before writing a single test.
Postman is where API exploration begins. Not where API testing ends.

It's the mindset shift most SDETs take years to make.

What was your "I didn't know what I didn't know" API testing moment?

I watched Reading FC's Head of AI talk through their strategy at Reading100 AI — one of the sharper transformation talks I've heard this year. Not because of the AI. Because of everything underneath it.

Some context: Stuart Fenton is the first person to ever hold the title "Head of AI" in English football at Reading FC.

Four things stood out — and none of them are really about AI.

𝟭. 𝗕𝗶𝗮𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗲𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗲 While bigger clubs are still running pilots and hiring consultants, Reading are already using it — in the scouting room, the analyst suite, the back office. Not a 2027 roadmap. Today.

𝟮. 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗶𝗴-𝗯𝗮𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘆 Scouting used to mean days of manual tagging and a shortlist built on whoever your network happened to know. Now a single query — find me a left-sided centre-back who progresses the ball like Player X, within budget, injury history below threshold Y — narrows 200,000+ professional footballers to a shortlist in an afternoon. AI narrows the field. Humans still pick the player.

𝟯. 𝗣𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹 "Algorithms don't sign contracts. Relationships do." Freeing analysts from manual tagging didn't shrink the team — it gave them their time back, to spend with coaches instead of a mouse.

𝟰. 𝗙𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽𝘀, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 Fans feedback is actively used to ground new development.

None of this is really a football story. It's what any transformation looks like when it's done well: act before you're certain, experiment in public, keep humans at the centre of the decisions that matter, and build the feedback loop with the people living the change — not around them.

It's the same pattern I keep finding underneath every transformation I look at, which is a big part of why I'm building a course around it.

Wipro Claims Big with AI: Art of Deception or Real Benefits? 

Wipro claims that AI freed up #productivity equal to 20,000 workers and redeployed all of them - no firing! 

I'd love to believe that number but the skeptic in me is holding me back.

Wipro's CTO Sandhya Ramachandran Arun says AI initiatives have delivered productivity gains "equivalent to the output of 20,000 employees," all reportedly redeployed and not let go. Over 100,000 of Wipro's ~243,000 employees (as of June) have gone through advanced AI training and certification.

Most media reports suggest Sandhya insisting this isn't "person-to-person replacement by an agent", it's the same engineer now managing agents, moved to other projects, or upskilled into a new role. 

To quote her (verbatim): "the shift has to be from productivity to outcomes."

However, here’s where my skepticism comes from. Wipro is the only company of India's top 4 IT firms that doesn't disclose AI-specific revenue. #TCS and #Infosys quantify it but Wipro doesn't.

And per Nord-IQ Research’s Manoj Chandra Jha, Wipro is still in the "cost-absorbing phase" of AI monetisation and the real test will come when "these deals start converting to revenue and margin recovery." He also notes Wipro's investment matches peers like TCS, Infosys and HCLTech, but it "trails in commercialization maturity."

This isn't happening in a vacuum. TCS is building toward 8,900 forward-deployed engineers, Infosys ~6,000, and Wipro says it'll land "in line with peers." The whole $315B Indian IT services industry is rewriting hiring and contracts around AI at once.

So, is it a genuine strategy from Wipro or just a soft landing narrative for a number that nobody can verify?

"20,000 workers' worth of productivity" is surely a compelling headline. But unfortunately it is unaudited, undefined, and comes with zero revenue disclosure to back it up. 

Redeployment certainly beats layoffs as a PR story but that doesn't make it the whole story.
